utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everybody in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, for the Office of the Prosecutor I'm Tom Hannis along with Selma Sakic and Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Slobodan Zecevic Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic and Aleksandar Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if there are no housekeeping matters, could the witness be escorted back to the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, to you, Mr. Planojevic. I remind you that you are still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry. Good morning to you, sir. I remind you are you are still on your oath. Mr. Hannis, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, before I start with my questions, just a couple of things. First, I have to complement you. Yesterday, you did such a good job of following the transcript on the screen before continuing your answer, but actually since I'm speaking in English and you are speaking in Serbian, it's not so important that you do it with me, but when you are asked questions on cross-examination if will be more important for you to wait for the transcript, and I understand from the interpreters that you can actually answer a little more quickly and not have to watch the transcript so much. It's just between question and answer. Thank you. And when we left off we had talked about April 4th and 5th. I need to try and speed up a little bit because I have a time-limit, so I'll try and ask you to keep your answers short where possible, and if you need more time to elaborate, please let me know. I want to ask you if on April 5th or 6th you and some of your fellow Serbian policemen went to the community centre in Vraca?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I need to explain how we set off that night. I won't take long, I'll give you a shortened version, if I may, on the 4th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, briefly, I was trying to understand what was going on that night. Around 11.30, that is 2330, I was informed that Jusuf Prazina, who was later one of the leaders of a military formation in Sarajevo, had broken into the police community centre and set up his headquarters there and later on the special unit had his headquarters there as well. I was also informed at the same time that at the police station where I was commander, some 30 armed Green Berets had forced their way into the police station, that they had broken open offices, and safes and then taken away what they wanted to. That all went on in the presence of the executives of other police stations. Still during the same night, I also found out that in Novo Sarajevo a policeman was killed who, by mere chance, came to that station to file a criminal report, he was a Serb. The shift commander who was also a Serb was knocked senseless with rifle-butts and both of them were take downstairs to the basement. One of them, whose name was Petrovic, was killed by a shot fired in the back of his head, whereas the other survived. His name was Lazar Bojanic and he told me everything about it. When he came to, Lazer Bojanic, that is, he went to see -- or went to the urgent medical ward, and on the way there he saw Ismet Dahic, the chief of the police station of Stari Grad, in Sarajevo, as well as Sakib Puskar. He was one of the chiefs of the Green Berets. I asked Suad Kadric over the phone who was at the police station, and I said that he was at the station in the evening to withdraw the Serb police officers from the ground to the station and mind them so that none get killed. He did that and in the morning some maybe as many as 10 people came to see me in my apartment. The same night I called up Sinisa Karan who was at Dolac Malta and he was the chief of the crime prevention service at the same station, I called him to come to my apartment. He called me up later and said that the cross roads Dolac Malta was blocked and that there was shooting so that he couldn't pass. He said that the Green Berets were shooting, or rather that they had blocked the crossroads. At the city SUP, the situation was the same, the Green Berets had forced their way into the premises, Sreten Zukovic was shot. He worked at the city SUP, he was a Serb, and according to his words, it was by mere chance that he survived. The man lives in the Netherlands these days and still suffers consequences from happened. And now I would move on to the part when we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, I can see that you have a very good memory for detail, but could you please tell us what happened after the ten or so people came to see you in your apartment and what you did next?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We sat in cars and had long-barrelled weapons with us and we set off for Vraca. Upon arrival, that's the local commune which is the lowest level socio-politico organisation. I found some police officers there and I mentioned that -- their three names, I believe it was the three of them who were there, and others too. There was Mirko Vuzolo [phoen], Ratko Novcic, and Radislav Milenkovic. They said to me that Momo Mandic and his brother had gone to the school to have the students come out in order to make room for the Serb Ministry of the Interior. At 1.00 we met into front of the local commune offices and some police officers who hailed from Pale, some of those who were with me, they asked whether they could go to see their families, and I let them go. We drove them to Tilava, which is perhaps 10 kilometres from Vraca in the direction of Jahorina, so they could go to Pale on a forest-path. They couldn't go by way of Sarajevo because there was already shooting. Some five of us returned from Tilava to Vraca. Upon arrival at Vraca we saw that nothing was happening and being hungry and it was afternoon around 1.00 we decided to go back to my apartment, which we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever go to the Vraca school on April 5th or 6th?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I set off on the 4th and I explained what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I understand, but did you ever go to the school itself or only to the community centre?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never entered the school compound. On the 5th, there was fighting but I expected that it would cease because I hoped that we would be able to enter the school compound peacefully. We spent the night in my apartment and on the 6th we all went back to Vraca, but my brother informed me that my wife wasn't well, she was pregnant at the time, and I drove those four or five people up to the school at Vraca and continued to Rogatica because my wife was there with her parents. I had to leave because she had problems with her pregnancy. And that's just a short account since we are short of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And when did you actually join your colleagues in what became the RS MUP?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived at Pale on the 13th privately to see what was happening, and I was in contact with Cedok Jajic [phoen] on that day. I had to go to Pionirska, that's in the outskirts of Sarajevo. And he asked me to see what was happening there because a reserve police station which later became a regular police station, and upon returning I informed him truthfully that there was nothing going on there. That was the 16th, I believe, it was a Friday, and we agreed that I should come back on Monday and join them at Vraca. At the time I was offered to be the chief of the centre, which was in Pionirska, but I wouldn't accept it due to my family commitments. I arrived at Vraca on the 19th of April, and as of that day I was a -- I was in my position there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you say you were offered the position as head of centre, you mean the CSB for Sarajevo, the job that Zoran Cvijetic held later on?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's Centar municipality. So it's not the Centar of security services, it's the Centar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So the job you were offered was to be the chief of Centar Sarajevo SJB?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And instead you were given the job of assistant minister for crime prevention and detection?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You say you started your work on the 19th of April?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where was that, in Pale?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I went to the Vraca school and until early June I was there. I'm not sure of the exact date, but my office was there at the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as I understand from your interview, you held that position as assistant minister until approximately the 21st, 22nd of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During those three months or so how many occasions did you have to actually meet with and speak with Mico Stanisic, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we met three times in that time-period. I suppose that I should elaborate when and on which occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. But before you do, let me ask you a question. Did you know Mico Stanisic before April of 1992? And if so, how did you know him?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the police secondary school we were the same generation in 1972, 1973. We worked at the city secretariat until my departure to Novo Sarajevo or until his departure to the economy. I believe that somewhere around 1985 he left the police to work in the economy. We knew each other well and we did judo, so on the occasion of police games we travelled to competitions together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So if you can begin, then tell me about the first time during your tenure as assistant minister that you had a meeting or discussions with Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember the exact date but it would have been in early May. I believe it was in the evening hours when the then minister arrived, Cedo Kljajic and I were present in my office, I think, and I think it's worth mentioning that during that conversation we requested that Momo Mandic, although there was no decision to that effect, he acted as a deputy minister, and we asked Mr. Stanisic that he be removed from the headquarters of the ministry. We explained to Stanisic that people with a shady past were around Momo Mandic, I'm referring to Branislav Vuletic, I believe his first name was Branislav, and Zeljko Skrba and they had reputation for stealing. I don't have to retell that conversation, but in essence, once we stated our reasons, the minister promised us he would do all he could to remove Momo. I believe only seven days elapsed and after that I never saw Momo on the premises again. Certainly not in the offices. And that was our first contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this took place in Vraca at the school?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: These two men you mentioned as having a shady past, Mr. Vuletic and Mr. Skrba, what kind of criminal activity did you understand them to be involved in?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they engaged in theft, car theft and other kinds of theft. It isn't documented but there was intelligence to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you have information at that time when you had this conversation with Mr. Stanisic about Mr. Mandic having a group of men, maybe as many as ten men, involved in taking cars from the TAS factory in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time mass theft from TAS hadn't yet begun. And I don't know that Mandic had these ten people to steal as many cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember being interviewed in 2004 by representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor in Banja Luka on the 8th and 9th of June, 2004?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 51 of the English transcript, let me read an answer you gave and ask if you remember saying this, first of all. At line 28: "And for that reason that's why we asked the minister to come and we asked Momo to be expelled from the ministry, but at that time he had already organised groups of, like, 10 -- groups of like 10 criminals who would take Golfs to Belgrade." Do you remember saying that back in 2004?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember giving a statement like that, but that could only happen later, not at the time we had our conversation. I know that Biljana Plavsic said at the Assembly that Momo organised that, but to my mind he couldn't have had ten people. However, referring to the period around the 1st of May, I believe that 270 Golfs were taken to the federal part of Sarajevo in all, but not as early as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You and Mr. Kljajic were concerned enough about Mr. Mandic and these associates and their activities to ask to have him removed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry to interrupt, but I believe that the last part of the answer was not recorded. The previous answer "I believe that 270 Golfs were taken to the federal part of Sarajevo in all," and then he explained what happened to the rest of the cars and that wasn't recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would prefer to deal with these matters, unless it's something that's necessary to have up on the screen now, by the usual process of having the tapes listened to and it appearing in the final transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Except, Mr. Hannis, that if in terms of the -- to have the witness's answer complete at this point, it may as well be dealt with now. I assume that Mr. Zecevic has only arisen because it is not insignificant, the part that is not recorded. So if the witness could be invited to repeat his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The difficulty, is, Your Honour, I'm going in the dark because I don't know what was said or not said. I don't know how they ask the question, but I will certainly ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Based on what you've heard Mr. Zecevic say, can you tell us if there was something additional you said and repeat it now?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question for me? I had intelligence that 270 Golfs had been taken to the federal part of Sarajevo until that time; whereas, the remainder were still in stock at TAS. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. Now, I was asking you about your request along with Mr. Kljajic that Mr. Mandic be removed from the Ministry of the Interior because of his association with these shady -- with these persons with what you described as a shady past and engagement in theft. Did you learn that upon leaving the Ministry of the Interior he had been appointed the minister of justice?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was your reaction to that? Did that cause you any concern, that somebody that you didn't think was appropriate to be a policeman because of his association with those types of gentlemen you described becoming the minister of justice? Did you express concern to the prime minister or anybody else?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, who was I to express concern. I had been expressing concern privately for a long time, but there was really no time to think about such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Tell us then, if you will, about the second time you had a conversation with Mico Stanisic in that April to July time-period when you were assistant minister?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember it was early June. There was an order to transfer the special unit whose headquarters was at the school at Vraca and to relocate all executive personnel so that they may devote themselves to operational work in the area of Pale and Jahorina. So they were meant to move from the school. A number of police officers from -- who were members of the centre were concerned that the Defence line could be broken, and there was some confusion, and I thought it appropriate to contact the minister and try to persuade him to keep at least part of that unit at the school. That's what I did. I went to Kosuta, as far as I remember, and I explained why I had come and that at least one platoon should remain. I believe that he accepted my reasons and that a platoon stayed behind at Vraca for the peace of mind of the people. Although, it was his opinion that most of the personnel should be dealing with the armed combat, which is indeed their duty under the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Page 11, 24 I would suggest that the witness repeats his answer because it was recorded quite contrary to what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, the last part of your answer was recorded that: "Although it was his opinion that most of the personnel should be dealing with the armed combat, which is indeed their duty under the law." And it's being suggested by Mr. Zecevic that what you actually said, and it seems logical, was that it was his opinion that most of the personnel should be dealing -- should not be dealing with armed combat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that they should go about their regular business. That's what I said. And the regular business was public law and order, crime enforcement, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Regular police work?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Policing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think you said there was at least one other conversation during that time-period, can you tell us about the third one, when and where was that and what topics did you discuss?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already during this conversation we touched on some subjects and another conversation was casual. I told you that we had met, if I remember correctly, I think it was during the departure from Bistrica, it's a hotel on Jahorina. So at the exit we met, it was an incidental encounter so, if you would like me to, I can describe it for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, please, and if you recall, approximately when this was?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to remember. It could have been in the second half of June. Judging by the chronology of events, I think that it should have been in the second half of the month of June. What I remember as striking was that Mico had a German Shepherd dog with him and I told him that he reminded me of a historical figure. This is why I remember that. This was more of a joke, and he told me that he was a friend as opposed to some other people. Maybe these jokes weren't that funny after all, but as I say, this is why I remember the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just out of curiosity, what historical figure were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is well known that Josip Bros during the Second World War, maybe it's somewhat inappropriate but our conversation was really true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Tell us what you talked about on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not really talk much on that occasion. I told you that at Kosuta on the second occasion, perhaps we touched on some other subjects, whereas on this particular occasion we didn't discuss anything important.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My misunderstanding then. Could we go back to the second conversation in early June at Kosuta, what additional topics did you talk about other than keeping some of the special unit at Vraca?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me go back to the first conversation as I think it's important, perhaps it wasn't clear from my first statement what we talked about when. On the occasion of our first meeting in Vraca, inter alia, even though there was not so much crime at the time, I was aware that without the use of armed force, I could not make any arrests, and therefore I asked the minister for his approval to engage my special unit if there was anything more serious and he said that there would be no problem if there was something that you couldn't resolve on your own, and I think that he then forwarded that to Karisik, that he told him that when I contacted him that I could use this special units. So I suppose as we touched on this, that you would return to this topic, so I thought I should mention it. On the occasion of the second conversation, as I had been absent from the ministry seat from the 8th to the 27th of May, as I got a child, my wife gave birth to my son in Belgrade and I was there looking after my son, and as some of the cars had been taken away from people who had stolen them, I told him that we would have to investigate this, somebody would have. Though it was not just police, but also Territorial Defence at the school in Vraca, they would come there to have breakfast and to spend the night. And in this conversation the then minister told me, all right, do what you can, however, be careful and let us finish with the combat, and what we cannot do now, try to document all the traces, make notes, and then we'll resolve it at a proper time. So I think this is what you were interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During that conversation, did you talk to him about any other particular crimes -- I am sorry, before I start that question, I want to ... Yes, in the last part of your answer, you were talking about it was: "Though it was not just police but also Territorial Defence at the school in Vraca, they would come there to have breakfast and spend the night. And in this conversation then the minister told me, all right, do what you can ..." Are you talking about the Territorial Defence people at the school in Vraca came to Kosuta? I'm not clear what you are referring to there.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't understand me properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't want to raise it before because I understand that I'm frustrating you, Mr. Hannis, but the whole answer between lines 9 and 21 was misinterpreted entirely. Or well, misinterpreted, the actual meaning what the witness wanted to say was not recorded. That is perhaps the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One of my great regrets in life so far is not having learned B/C/S and this is very difficult. We have interpreters, professionals in the booth to do this job. I understand Mr. Zecevic's frustration in hearing things that he knows or believes are not right, but when he raises this, I don't know how to deal with it other than to ask the witness to repeat his whole long answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, it has nothing to do with my frustration, I was just, I see that you are confused with the answer and you are confused with the answer because it wasn't recorded as it was said. So maybe the witness should be instructed to speak slower so the interpreters will have the time to properly pick up what he said and translate that. Thank you. And interpret that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And if I may add, the witness himself from the last thing he said, it is obvious that he is -- that the confusion is -- that there's reason for the confusion, let me put it that way. So although it's time consuming, Mr. Hannis, there seems to be no alternative but to go back to the question and ask the witness, as Mr. Zecevic has suggested, to speak slowly so the interpreters can accurately convey what he intends to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll do that, Your Honour. And I trust the interpreters will do as they usually do, request the witness to slow down if they are having difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On the occasion -- well, let me break it down into a couple parts because I want to address part of your answer. At the beginning you mentioned talking to the minister about wanting to engage the special unit sometimes for the needs of your job as assistant minister for crime prevention and detection, and you said you asked the minister for his approval and he said there would be no problem. Is it correct that the Minister Stanisic is the person who had authority to decide when and how a special unit could be used?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now let me go to the second part of your answer. You were talking about on the occasion of the second conversation and you mentioned you had been absent for about three weeks from the 8th to the 27th of May because your wife had given birth to your second child; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then the answer is put in the transcript as saying "... as some of the cars had been taken away from people who had stolen them, I told him we would have to investigate this." Is that correct, you are telling Mico Stanisic about some of the problems with the stolen cars?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the cars were seised from the thieves and left at the school complex, and then they disappeared from there. And that was why because the members of the Territorial Defence would come to the complex to have breakfast, and I'm not certain but maybe they also slept there, I wanted simply to have some order and to register the people entering and exiting and then to try to find out who had stolen these two cars, so that was the essence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So in connection with those cars you had some suspicion that you thought it might have been somebody from the Territorial Defence that had taken them?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been police as well, because the police was also not immune to such actions, but I thought that there should be some order and that we should have records about who was entering, which had not been the case until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your conversation though, I take it that from your interview in 2004 that you expressed concern about more than just a couple of stolen cars, that you had a concern that crime was widespread and that you weren't getting all the information about that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember now. I apologise, I'm under stress somewhat even now. It's possible that on the occasion of our third meeting we discussed about the issue of Batica, I'm not certain. When I say Batica, I mean Vlahovic, I cannot remember his first name. It was a man for whom I had information which I received in Belgrade that he was committing certain crimes in the area, down in Grbavica which is below Vraca. Do you need any clarifications about how I received this information and how the conversation between me and Stanisic was developing?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, let me ask you a couple of specific questions. This person that you refer to as Batica, was he also referred to sometimes as Batko? You'll have to answer out loud?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm confusing them, I think it's one in the same person. Batko, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand he was a former boxer?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was how he introduced himself. In the beginning of the war, he was on camera wearing a Serbian cap and this is something I remember as striking. He was a short man and it was said that he had engaged with boxing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is it fair to say in some ways he was sort of a one-man crime wave, alleged to have been involved in a number of rapes, armed robberies, killings?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some indicia, and I can tell you how I came to this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first information, I was in Belgrade and I met with a friend of mine, Goran Vuksanovic who used to work in Sarajevo before, and he told me that this Batko had been in Belgrade and that he heard him talk about carrying out liquidations in the Sarajevo area. So upon my return from Belgrade, I thought it appropriate to interview a man who was a Sarajevo native who was from my department, Zoran Mihajlovic, I knew him before the war and he was well versed in this area and I wanted to ask him if he knew anything about this. He told me that rumours were going about that Batica would take people from their apartments and probably as no one could report that these people had gone missing, that had not reached us as yet at that point. Thinking about the problem, and he was a member of paramilitary, there were always 10 or so problematic people and he was a deviant personality, mentally, as far as I knew, and I then mentioned this to the minister. I asked him what should be done about this man, it should be investigated, this whole matter. In the conversation we agreed that we should alert the army because he was a member of the armed forces. The minister on his part said that he would call the Main Staff, and he told me please follow this and see whether anything will really be done about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who -- in the first part of your answer you said he was a member of paramilitary and then you said later on that you and the minister agreed that you should alert the army because he was a member of the armed forces. Those seem to be inconsistent. What was your information that he was actually a member of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He used to go into combat and he was wearing a uniform. It's difficult to distinguish now what was the army and what were the paramilitaries. Probably both are correct. This is why I'm confusing them. Whether he was a member of the army or a member of a paramilitary unit, but he was a member of armed formations that used to go into armed combat. If he ever really participated in combat indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you follow the situation with him? Do you know -- well, first of all let me ask you, do you know if Minister Stanisic actually called the army or the army Main Staff about Batko?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. But if you want another clarification, because there was another person that I discussed the subject with, maybe you will get a more complete picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We will come to that conversation in a little bit. Let me ask you this question: Do you know if Batko was ever arrested or detained after this conversation with the minister?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the man disappeared for ten or 15 days and he was not in the area at all, this Batko, I mean. And when he appeared, the army arrested him, when I say the army, I know exactly that he was in Lukavica in prison there and I'm not sure for how long he was detained, but later on I heard that he had been released once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And that release was also in 1992? He wasn't detained very long; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not for long.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me turn to a couple of other individuals for a moment. Did you know Stojan Zupljanin in 1992? And if so, can you tell us when and how you first met him?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met Stojan Zupljanin at a collegium in Belgrade. It was on the 11th of July, 1992. Until then I had not seen him physically.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you have any personal dealings with him in 1992 other than seeing him at that meeting in Belgrade on July 11th?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have any dealings with him until that time, I mean direct dealings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And after that in 1992, any dealings?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we would meet later even when we went skiing on Mount Jahorina during the war, I mean, and also in Pale we would meet each other, and I think that perhaps since September 1993 we also met in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where were you working in 1994, if I may ask?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In state security service which was then called the National Security Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you know or did you hear about Mr. Zupljanin being appointed Internal Affairs advisor to the president of the RS in 1994?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard, but I really couldn't tell when that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to ask you about Branko Djeric, the prime minister of the RS from April or May until about November of 1992. Can you tell us when and how you first met him?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have known Mr. Branko Djeric for a long time, long since the war. We were born close to Rogatica, both of us, and we practically know each other from our native village. Later on he was a professor at the faculty of economy in Sarajevo and we met on several occasions and we were on quite good terms with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you tell us about your first meeting with him in 1992 after you were in your position of assistant minister?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We met at the Bistrica hotel. It was the seat of the government and therefore also the seat of the prime minister. I got there to have coffee, because one could come by and have a drink, with the professor and neighbour and friend Vaso Dragovic, and they were colleagues because they worked at the same faculty. And then Vaso also called professor or rather Prime Minister Djeric to join us so that we could have coffee together and we did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did you discuss at that first meeting?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think about problems, there was quite a lot of confusion which was normal considering the conditions, nothing was functioning, there were large-scale thefts already and many other things were going on. I'm not certain if it was on that occasion, but it probably was, that I proposed that the government should put something in writing for its part, so that it would allow the police to be more efficient. I believe that the government needed to make some decisions and take some measures which would regulate certain areas. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As Djeric was a scientist and not well versed with state administration, he asked me to try and jot down what these decisions could be and how they should be formulated. I accepted this. I found Slobodan Skipina believing that he was a man who was good in writing, that he would know how to formulate it well, and so we wrote a memo together, it had about four points and the essence was that the government should take certain decisions, primarily I think to make a list of strategic goods that were in stock, then who could have them at their disposal so that we could have record of that because there was oil and wheat and so on in reserves, but nobody knew what the stocks were because the records had been left in the federal part. So in this memo, we wrote down what the government should do and later on I brought it to him. I'm not sure how long after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know if you indicated, do you recall when that first meeting took place, approximately?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was probably also in May, but it's difficult to place everything within a precise time-frame. Sometimes I can't say the exact date because certain later connotations that the events had, but sometimes it's just approximately. I suppose it was in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that. You mentioned getting together with Slobodan Skipina to write up these recommendations. That's the Slobodan Skipina who was the head of state security in the RS MUP at the time?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he was the chief of national security at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know why -- why Mr. Djeric would be talking to you two or, well, I guess talking to you rather than to the minister Mr. Stanisic himself about this?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose because we were in such a situation where we talked but perhaps he could give you a proper explanation. It was an informal chat and these were problems that I was directly responsible for, I mean, the crime. And probably this was also one of the reasons why.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, you mentioned in your earlier answer that one of the things you discussed at that first meeting was the large-scale thefts. Did you have any other discussion in your meetings with Mr. Djeric in 1992 about any other kinds of crimes?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that when I brought him this paper it was probably in early June or thereabouts, that I also touched on this again because it all happened within ten days, the conversation with the minister and then when the prime minister. I mentioned Vlahovic once again and I believed that we would have to go all the way up to the state leadership perhaps in order to resolve this problem. I think that it was perhaps four or five days after my conversation with the minister, not more. And I touched on this subject as well and he asked me what should be done, and I told him well, the minister would call the guys at the command, but perhaps it would be good if the state leadership should intervene or perhaps you, as the prime minister, should also call the command. In my presence, but I cannot be certain whether he called directly the then president Radovan Karadzic or whether he called the command, but he made a phone call and he requested that the issue be resolved. And soon after that, as I told you, the arrest took place and therefore I did not continue to follow this problem anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you're referring to Batko or Batica?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I told you Vlahovic, Batko.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next if we could show the witness Exhibit 1D46.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, on your screen in a moment will be a document I think you saw during proofing. It's an order dated the 15th of May, 1992, from the Minister Mico Stanisic about forming war units in the RS MUP. Do you recall having seen this?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I forgot my glasses, so take my apologies, but I hope I'll be able to read it even without. Anyway, I know the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can go to the second page in both English and B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- Mr. Cvijetic is kindly donating his glasses to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was reading last night and yet I forgot.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will recognise that this is not the first time. I have a pair that I rent out to witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: For a small price.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Could you look at item number 9, I don't know if you can see the number 9 on the B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it. It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And my English translation says in order to command and control the overall forces of the ministry, a staff shall be established comprising, and the following list of people. We see assistant ministers for crime, police, communications and crypto-protection, materiel and finance are members. I take it assistant minister for crime, that was you; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember being informed that you were going to be a member of this staff?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly I was informed subsequently. From the 8th of May until the 27th I was absent. Somebody, possibly Cedo Kljajic, related this order to me in a conversation when I returned from Belgrade which would have been in late May early June and informed me that I was a member of that staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Am I correct though that you in your administration never had occasion to command anyone in combat in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't command anyone nor did I know how to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could look at the top of the page, there's item number 7, it talks about the use of the ministry units in co-ordinated actions with the armed forces. Do you remember reading that paragraph before? Actually that entire item number?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could go to the top of the B/C/S page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see it, yes, I'm reading it. I can't give you a precise answer. I may have read it. It's been a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Having read it now, can you tell us if that description of how coordination between the MUP and the army would take place in connection with combat actions is consistent with your experience of how it actually happened in 1992? If you had any knowledge or experience about how it actually worked.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know how it was supposed to be because we all had defence plans and the defence plans outlined what should be done in any situation, whether they were extraordinary circumstances, imminent threat of war, in case of imminent threat of war, or war, the units are resubordinated to military commands and combat would be carried out in co-ordinated action with the armed forces. When I say resubordination, that means that they are placed under the command of the units to which they belong. The police, and I'm speaking about a small number of members before the war, even if we were to take all of them together, I wouldn't -- they wouldn't be -- they couldn't make up a division. And you asked me how it all worked. As far as I know, there were problems. At the beginning there was no military really. It was established on the 12th or the 15th of May. There wasn't much combat, but there were some ad hoc skirmishes and some fighting. So at that moment there was nobody to resubordinate to. When you were attacked, you would seek to protect your own life and that was it. But I heard from colleagues because I didn't get involved except when I had to, and I think I stated that I may have taken part in combat once or twice. The police would be placed in the most inconvenient places. We would say that we would be set up because we were susceptible to being cut off and destroyed and that's when -- that was a problem. So the minister insisted that the police not be sent to combat whenever it could be avoided, but instead the reserve forces would take over and the police would be involved in combat only when strictly necessary and unavoidable and otherwise should go about their regular policing work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I have on that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next I'd like to show you Exhibit P568.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, the next one coming up on the screen is a document that you will recognise dated the 5th of June, 1992, from you to the CSB centres. Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what we call a dispatch in our lingo, but if we consider the way it was dispatched, it can be considered a letter because a dispatch has to be encrypted and sent over dedicated lines, but this was sent out through couriers and by telefax and that is not really how it should be. So we can see it as a letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the substance of this was directing the CSBs to do what? If you can just give me a short summary.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as it says here, by the end of May there has been a surge of crime against property, but also war crimes and all members are ordered to combat this energetically, and then it says how they should go about it, conduct on-site investigations, and if they were unable to implement radical measures such as placing somebody in custody and so on, that evidence should be collected and once the conditions are ripe, the perpetrators should be prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned that it says that there had been a significant increase in property crime and war profiteering and it says "and especially in war crime"; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could put up on the screen 1D84, and what I'd like to do, if it's possible, is to have the B/C/S versions of both the current exhibit and 1D84 so the witness can do a comparison?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The next one that's going to come up, I hope, on the right side of your screen is also -- appears to be the same dispatch or letter from you to the CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could scroll to the bottom on the left so we can see the signature block and the signature of -- actually, I need to see the signature block and the signature of both pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise the signature on either one or both of those?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that both the signatures are mine. The letter D is a bit funny, but the last name as written here Planojevic is certainly my signature. The D is a bit strange though.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you'll see in the typewritten block above the typewritten signature, in the document on the left we see the B/C/S word Za, Z-a, appears twice in that block but only once in the one on the right, so these appear to be two different documents; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you help us with that? Did you sometimes prepare duplicate originals because they had to be transmitted to different locations by different means?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. This happened because, as I said, that we use couriers because communications lines were down and there wasn't a sufficient number of copies, so it was retyped. Mico Orasan [phoen], Petko Pekic, who all when they went to the field took some copies with them for every police station, because sometimes the chief of the centre was unable to contact the police stations because there were no communications lines. That may have been the reason. And there is really -- I don't see why anybody would try to make a forgery. So possibly there wasn't a sufficient number of hard copies, so that's why it was retyped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, just looking at these two versions it strikes me that the signatures seem to be quite different. Are they really yours, both of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Planojevic certainly is my signature, but the D, I'm not sure about that. If you look at the last letter of my signature, I believe you will see that it's the same and I write it in a particular way. Here the left-hand signature begins with a D and I believe it's the same on my identity card. Planojevic certainly is my signature, but the D, again, is strange, as if it were not my handwriting, but then why should anybody ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's a different question but I mean, I'm sure that you would be able immediately to recognise a handwritten signature as being yours, and so my question is just if you can recognise both of these signatures as being yours written by yourself because they appear to be very different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I answered you a minute ago. I'm convinced that Planojevic is my signature, I'm not sure about the D. Now I can't really --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just one more question, I guess, before the break, if I may. Just from looking at these two documents, is there any way you can tell how either one of them was transmitted? There's nothing on there indicating delivery information, is there? There's no fax header on it or there's no delivery stamp on the bottom? There's no way to tell, is there?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were functioning under the given circumstances. It was hard to come by a typewriter and there was no protocol department, there was no stamp. So we had to make due with what we had and that's how we went about it. We tried to do as much as we could under the circumstances. What you say is correct, in a well-organised state that would not be permissible, but we had to start from scratch.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is a good time for the break for me, if it's convenient for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We rise and return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Welcome back, witness. I want to ask a few more questions about the dispatch that's on the screen. In your administration for crime prevention and detection in 1992, did you maintain any kind of communications log-book for in-going and out-going documents?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was head of the administration I don't remember that there was one. Maybe when we moved from Vraca to Kalovita Brda, maybe there was something like that but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I note on this document there's no Registry number, if that's the correct term. I know we see on some other MUP documents that there will be a number usually above the date line, you know what I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know. There should be something like that under the rules of clerical work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: With regard to your work in the ministry as an assistant minister, was there a rule or requirement about copying the minister or informing the minister about dispatches sent out by you as an assistant minister, and/or about documents that you received?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister should be informed of everything important, everything essential.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know if he was informed about this dispatch that you sent out? And if so, how was that done?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say with certainty whether he was informed, but one copy should have been sent to the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could next show the witness Exhibit 1D85. 1D85.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: However these two documents may have gone out, it appears that your message did get out to the field at least in some places. You'll see 1D85 is a document, a dispatch dated 8 June 1992 from the CSB in Banja Luka to all SJBs under that centre. And it's basically forwarding your dispatch that we were just looking at. Have you seen this before?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you see this one has what I've been referring to as a Registry number above the date line?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And to the right of that I have in parentheses "dx," it's my understanding that's some kind of designator regarding the urgency of the document; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall now what "dx" stood for?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It stands for urgent. There is just one level above this, very urgent, which was required to be delivered within two hours. And this is the second most urgent dispatch. This -- the Banja Luka centre obviously had an intact encryption centre because in Banja Luka there had been no combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what the time limit was for delivering an urgent document?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. A day, two days maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's all right. I think we've got some communication witnesses who have talked about that and will talk about that. During your time as assistant minister for crime prevention, did you receive reports from the field from any SJBs or CSBs during that April to July time-period.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember receiving any documents except if it was handed to me personally. Cedo Kljajic and me stayed for some time -- were in Vraca, but everything went to Kosuta at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you moved from Vraca to Pale when, approximately?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably around the 5th of June or between the 5th and the 7th of June. I think that was the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you were in Pale, did you receive any reports from the field and from your interview I'll mention a couple of specific locations to see if that refreshes your memory, Bratunac and Sekovici?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had contacts which were physical with people. They would come to see me. There was a man from Bratunac. I think his name was Makso. He was an experienced investigator and he would come to consult me about what to do and how. He would bring some notes about on-site investigations for me to inspect whether they were good, and from Sekovici, I think there was Goran --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once again for purpose of consultations to exchange experiences with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the interpreter asked if you could repeat the last name of the second person. Goran?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pilipic. P like as in Pale, he would also come to see me for consultation and to exchange experiences. Other forms of communication were not operational, [indiscernible] nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So if I understand correctly, you were getting oral reports from these men, not written reports?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orally and also records of on-site investigations. This Makso came to see me so that I could check if it was all, if there was anything else that needed to be recorded because there was no one else he could rely on. There were few people who were dealing with these matters in the field and I knew that he was doing it well so I told him that there were no problems, but I told him that he would have to involve judges in the on-site investigations whenever possible, especially if there were any cases of war crimes, and that they should always try to involve someone from the medical profession, the doctors, so that they would provide the descriptions. This is what I suggested to him during the conversation. As for the rest, I could see that he had done it well. I apologise. Yes, I understand. I sent some inspectors to provide assistance because they were more experienced.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During your time as assistant minister, did you ever receive in writing any reports or Official Notes about any war crimes?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any oral reports about war crimes?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just let me think for a bit. On one occasion I set off for Ilijas. I was explaining to you that I was in Vogosca and Ilidza, and so I was going in the direction of Ilijas. One of the police officers recognised me, I think he was called Cedo, and he was working somewhere in the Sarajevo area. And he mentioned one Mico, he said that rumours were going about that he would enter houses and it was possible that he would take people away. I think that this was a man who was not a local, he had come from somewhere in Serbia. So this is an oral report that I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: During your three months or so as assistant minister, I think you've already answered this in part, you were aware of massive car thefts from the TAS factory in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you personally go to Vogosca or send some of your workers there to try and do something about it?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Individuals did go there. Perhaps on the first or 2nd June I went there in person to Vogosca, Ilidza, and Ilijas. On that occasion, I also held a meeting in Vogosca with the people who were most responsible including the president of the Executive Board and brigade commander for the area. The chief of the station was not there because he had been wounded by a local criminal, and so a lower-ranked commander from the station was there. So I told him briefly about all problems. I told him that I was coming from the level of the state with all authority, that I was authorised by the state leadership and the ministry, and that something had to be done about this, especially as concerned the car thefts and the misappropriation of other more important goods or resources. The TAS and Pretis compounds were secured by the army at the time. I think that the commander was one Major Skipina. It's interesting that while we were still at the meeting, this Skipina came along and told his commander Vukovic that one Pena, who was a local criminal, had taken away I believe 10 or 20 Golfs on that very day. I insisted with the commander because the army secured it that this had to be resolved on that day. However, judging by his conduct, I understood that he did not have sufficient courage to get involved with this. And so I wouldn't take up much time, upon my return two or three inspectors tried to organise something because I think there was just one man from the crime prevention administration and he was well versed in the job, but he couldn't do anything because I think there were many so-called intervention units there. So from the administration level immediately after this it went. I apologise, when I was coming back from Ilidza, I just remember that now, there was one platoon of Special Police or I came along their commander, I met him somewhere on the road between Vogosca and Ilidza. His name Brdaric or, rather, Brdar, Zlatko Brdar, and I asked him where he was going. He told me that one platoon had been sent in order to maintain some order in this area, that is to say, in Ilidza. So upon my return, I'm not sure whether it was 3 or 4 or 5 people from the crime prevention administration with all instructions about what they should do; however, not much time passed, maybe 2 or 3 days at the most, they returned and told me that they were threatened down there and they did not dare to stay down there any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who were those individuals by name, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One that certainly went there was Simo Tusevljak, Milos Civcic as well, perhaps Nikola Milanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall who they said they were threatened by and in what way they were threatened?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One Boro Radic, he was a local, well, a man with a shady criminal past and he was the head of an intervention unit. They were deployed at a park. There was also another group mentioned which was not from the Vogosca area at all, they had come from somewhere else, and this Boro Radic also wounded Boro Maksimovic, the chief of the station, when the other tried to do something. That happened before. And the chief of the station was already on sick leave at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you say Boro Radic was the head of an intervention unit, what formation did that intervention unit belong to? Was it to the army, to the police, was it a paramilitary, do you know?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were recorded as army so they were comprised by armed formation, but I don't think they were under anyone's command and that the commander Vukota couldn't order them anything. They were in the park. At the time they had their own security and they were independent. I only think that they would be involved when they needed to join the combat but otherwise they wouldn't stand anyone ordering them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: A question about jurisdiction if you know the answer, who would have the authority to arrest and prosecute Boro Radic, whatever formation he belonged to, for the crime of shooting a police chief? Would that be the army, the police, both, do you know?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Essentially, not even in peacetime or in war time civilian police could not arrest military personnel. According to the law, if he would be found while committing the crime, he would be taken to custody and then handed over to military organs. That would be in peacetime. In war time it was implied that if a state functioned properly, that the army and the military prosecution organs should deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As a practical matter, if a policeman observed an army member committing a crime, a serious crime like a crime against life and limb in front of himself, could he not detain that person and then hand them over to the military authorities?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, according to peacetime regulations, probably that also pertained to war time but I'm not sure because we had no regulations at the time, but I know that according to defence plans it was so because a state of war had not been declared, one should have acted in the same manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we next show the witness Exhibit 1D106.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you've told us about I think you said this was in early June when you first went to Vogosca and met with Major Skipina and others and then your men came back in a few days saying that they had been threatened. This next document is a report dated the 12th of July about events, I think, between 3 and 10 or -- between the 3rd and the 12th of July. Do you recall seeing this before?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You showed me this document. I had not seen it before, but this is not the group that I had in mind. Later on they went there again. I think it was Milenko Karisik and Nikola, as far as I remember. It was the second occasion in which they went there, not the first one for which I said three or four of them went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I understand. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I would like the usher to assist me in handing you a hard copy, I think it will be easier to work with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, that's the point I want to make. This was a second effort to deal with some of the problems in Vogosca. If you look at the last page, I think you did mention the names of those two persons who were trying to deal with the situation and who wrote this report. Did you know them and who they worked for?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Karisik and Ljubinko Mitrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were employees of the crime prevention service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At what level? With the administration or with an SJB or the centre?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not certain anymore because within the centre throughout the month of May they had no operatives, no places were filled and we tried to overcome this situation. They would try to find people by going out into the field, people who could do the work, and I think that it's possible that in July they had already left the level and that some men had already been organised as part of the centre. So it's probably that they were at the centre level, I suppose, then under the command of the centre chief already.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And just to be clear, this Karisik is Milanko with an A and he is not the same person as Milenko who was head of the special unit am I right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's another man. Milanko and Milenko, they are different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You remember when you looked at this during proofing this was another effort to try and sort out the problem from the cars being stolen from the TAS factory, and it mentions that there was a meeting organised with some of the locals and that the chief, Mr. Maksimovic, was not there and returned on the 9th of July. It mentions that Nikola Milanovic, that's on page 2 for you, it's the bottom of page 1 of the English, came to Vogosca and he was reported to by these two gentlemen who wrote this report. Milanovic worked for you in your administration; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the administration, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then at the top of the second page in English and I think in the middle of your second page, it mentions that Dobro Planojevic arrived in Vogosca and that these two gentlemen met with you and told you about what they had observed and that you agreed that a crime service should be set up with certain persons named there, including Brane Vlaco and others. Do you remember? It's on the back, yeah, it's two-sided.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only see it now, so can you please bear with me for a moment so that I can have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Certainly. Take your time.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't remember this but it's obvious that it did take place because people wouldn't have imagined it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Even though you don't remember it?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, actually, they reported to me. They came up and told me this and they agreed that a department should be formed down there. But it wasn't down in Vogosca but rather in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For the purpose of investigating the situation of the cars stolen from TAS or at least partly for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me this as a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only for that reason, but to try and deal with the situation in general. It wasn't only the Golfs that were a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What were some of the other problems?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was citizens property and then that policeman told me that some 10 kilometres away those Mice guys were appearing, and the situation had to be improved in all respects. There was theft and stuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Also the problem with the police chief being shot?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really didn't know how that happened because that man wasn't in the area of Vogosca. I don't know how the shooting came about. He was a Karate fighter and I heard that this Boro shot, that there was a quarrel, and this Boro guy went for treatment and he was away for a month or so. Boro, although he was a station chief, never really appeared. I didn't see him throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you look at the -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just for the clarity of transcript. There might be a problem later on because the witness uses Boro for both the chief of the police station and for the criminal who committed the shooting because they actually are both Boros, so this would need to be clarified. I am sorry for interrupting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Which Boro was the Karate fighter?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both. But Boro Maksimovic was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that clears it up.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So Boro Maksimovic who was a station chief was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you could look at the third page of the document you have there, and we see that there was a meeting, the chief called for the 10th of July apparently, and at that meeting people expressed strong criticism of the MUP and the CSB, and the chief said the only appropriate -- the only people appropriate for work were members of the police of the Vogosca public security station. And then Chief Maksimovic said: "Almost every one of his police employees had stolen a Golf, which can be seen, but they would return them if anyone ever asked them to do so." Did you know about this? Did Karisik and Mitrovic tell you about this or did you -- I think you said you had not seen this report before, but did you learn about that statement by the SJB chief in Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you see, this was written on 12 July. On 11 July the colleagues were in Belgrade and I stayed until the 18th or 19th. Upon return on the first working day upon my return, I handed in my resignation. So I haven't seen this particular document before, but I think that Boro's statement says it all, there's no need for me to comment about them being -- being good police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The Brane Vlaco who is mentioned as being proposed to be part of the crime service that was going to be set up is listed as a current employee of the Sarajevo CSB. We've heard evidence about another Brane Vlaco who was associated with the prison in Kula I think. Is this a different man? Do you know both of them? It's on page 2 for you.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know both. Brane Vlaco who worked on white-collar crime in the city SUP. He was the one who was -- who they were proposing for the position in crime prevention and detection. He went to the SDK and later on became the director of the Raiffeisen Bank. Another Brane Vlaco is a man whom I know from the pre-war special unit. I believe this is about him. And I told you I had seen that man on 8 June at Kalovita Brdo. He told me that somebody had made an appointment for him to meet the minister, and, as I understood it, he was to become the deputy chief or the commander of the Vogosca station. After 20 minutes or half an hour of the conversation, somebody called him on that phone at headquarters from Vogosca saying that there was fierce fighting going on in Vogosca so he sat in his car and drove back. I don't know what later happened to that man, whether he ever actually took up his position in the police hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This report on the first page you'll see it appears directed to the SRBH minister of the interior, and then it says chief of the Romanija Birac CSB Sarajevo. From your knowledge at the time would this report have gone to the minister?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he was informed because we can see his name there, so I can assume as much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at the time the theft of cars from the TAS factory was a hot topic in the Ministry of the Interior, was it not?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was actually being tackled very seriously because we had already come by a floppy disk with the stock, so we -- and we knew how many cars this was about. And the government also discussed that later. However, I believe that this remained topical throughout the war. There were also seizures on the border or in police stations, but I cannot speak about the final outcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I want to go to the 11th of July and a meeting in Belgrade we've mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we bring up Exhibit P160.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, you know the meeting I'm referring to. You attended that meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And your name appears in this document with comments that you apparently made at the time. Have you seen that --
