utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, I guess for your convenience if we could show the witness page -- first of all page 19 in the B/C/S, page 18 of the English. I'm not sure I have the right page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's page 16 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And it's on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, 19 is the e-court page number. It's numbered 16 at the top in B/C/S. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the bottom, that's your name, at the bottom of the B/C/S page?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could then turn to the following page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You looked at this before, and do you have any disagreement with these remarks being attributed to you? Is this basically what you said at the meeting? Talking about the importance of reporting crimes, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's basically it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think the next to the last item it mentioned that it was -- that the documenting of war crimes is a priority. Is that what you said then?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, after this meeting on the 11th of July, did you have another occasion to speak with Mico Stanisic that we haven't talked about in detail before?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon returning from Belgrade when I resigned, there was a clash and that's probably what you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am. Can you tell us where that meeting took place and who was there?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was at the Bistrica hotel. One of the personnel officers behind the counter, or rather behind the bar of the hotel. There was Mr. Mico Stanisic, who was minister, and Momcilo Mandic and I also entered that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us briefly what that conversation was about?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the collegium in Belgrade I stayed with my family until Monday. It must have been the 18th or the 19th. Upon arrival at Pale, I was informed that the minister wanted to see me and that I should report to him urgently. They told me that he was at the Bistrica hotel and as I said, at the front desk they told me where he was to be found. I entered the room, I greeted the minister and Momcilo Mandic, and I said I'm reporting to you. I don't need to go into all the details so I'll give you a digested version. The minister asked me angrily where I had been for several days and how dare I be absent for that long and some expressions were used that I don't care to repeat now, and I replied in an irritated fashion, possibly impolitely, and there was an exchange between the two of us. Among others, he said the situation in your area is such and such and I said to him that I had warned everybody of my commitments to my family when I took over my position. And he said well you spend more time in Belgrade than I. And it escalated to the verge of a physical fight. But Momcilo Mandic stood between us and before leaving the room I only uttered a few swear words and I said that I wouldn't -- that I wouldn't hear of that whole department or of the crime situation ever again. And this is a -- this would be it in a nutshell because I don't want to take any more of your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you happen to know why Mr. Mandic, who was then the minister of justice, was present for this meeting?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not a meeting, sir. I simply reported to him. They were sitting there informally, Momo and Mico, so why shouldn't he be sitting there because we were -- we belonged to the same generation and we had known each other very long.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I add an additional explanation. Yes? I told to the then minister that he was more in Belgrade than I and that would resurface later, but that was said in anger because I had only seen him three times in that period. I actually shouldn't have said that to him because probably I spent more time in Belgrade than he. At the very beginning of the war, his family was in Herceg-Novi, I just wanted to add that because you may see a contradiction there and perhaps you would ask questions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you for that. So that was, I think, you said on the 17th or 18th. When did you actually have your last day on the job as assistant minister? Did you attend at another meeting later that week before you officially left?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The minister's collegium was called because I insisted that somebody must be appointed as new head of the administration. So in two days this collegium took place and I attended it. That's when I was officially relieved of duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who took over your job?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In essence, the minister asked me who is your deputy. He did so at the collegium. I didn't have a deputy and the only executive staff was the coordinator Goran Macar, and the minister told him at that meeting to start acting in my position until the matter is resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. So after the 20th or 21st, 22nd July when this meeting was held, what did you do then? Were you no longer working for the MUP? Did you try to retire? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I asked for a consensual termination of service, but then I knew that the army could mobilise me. However, on -- during a later conversation, the minister told me not to be a fool and not to ask for termination of service. He told me to have some rest and then we would see what we would do. So for a month or two for my private obligations because my mother-in-law had gone missing in Sarajevo, and I contacted some of my colleagues in the federal [indiscernible]. Several times a week I would have telephone conversations with them, so that was what I was mostly doing. I'm not sure whether it was in September when Dragan Kijac offered that I should move to the national security sector and that's how I started working there. Probably that was in September. Though you won't find any documents about that, about my request to terminate service or my re-assignment. I don't think such documents exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Dragan Kijac in September was the head of the state security of the RS MUP; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the head of the national security sector, it was called the national security but essentially that was the state security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I forgot that the name changed at some point. And he had taken over the job that previously had been held by Slobodan Skipina?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Slobodan Skipina was first and after him Dragan Kijac came to this position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was your job or position within the national security when you first started?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning there were some thoughts to establish an administration for subverting the economic base of society, so basically that was white-collar crime at the fiscal level. On my insistence this administration was never established there for practical reasons. Then there was another idea to have the administration for secret surveillance and we had started that, I had selected a number of men, but this administration for objective reasons never really came into being. We did not have sufficiently educated personnel, we had no premises, so basically I was working as an inspector up until the 1st of July, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what happened then on the 1st of July 1994, just in terms of your work career?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of service appointed me as the chief of the national security sector at the Sarajevo centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did you eventually retire from the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I retired twice. The first time on the 30th of May, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then I take it you came back since you said you retired twice. Tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I came back. After a verbal conflict with a colleague where prime minister was also present in 2000, I just left demonstrably. I judged that is just the kind of person I am and then ten months later I returned again to be the head of the same service, and then I retired on the 31st of December 2004. And after that I found employment somewhere else after a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to jump around a little bit and ask you about some individual episodes or incidents of certain crimes that I think you have some knowledge of based on your interview in 2004. You mentioned a policeman and I have a hard time pronouncing this name, I think it's Plajavaljecic [phoen]. Do you know who I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mladen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Can you tell us about him and what experience you had with him?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just mentioned it in passing as an example, I said that policemen also used to steal. It was an incident, I think somebody took something from somebody else and because I learned of this, I asked through Cedo Kljajic that such people be dismissed from police. Cedo did that, probably through the commander, and very soon this man began to work for the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I take it this happened during 1992, and if so, can you tell us approximately when?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably in May or June, later on I think that he left and went somewhere abroad. It was certainly not after June.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Cedo Kljajic at that time was head of public security in the RS MUP?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he was the main man for public security.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You also mentioned in that interview in 2004 a Muslim couple, I think, named Dilberovic and something that happened to them in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not Dilberovic. I'll help you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who committed this act were Dilberovic. As I was up at the seat, and we slept there practically, in the evening one of the police officers from my previous station called me and told me that in the area of Lukavica, which is again one of the suburbs of Sarajevo, a crime had taken place and that two persons had killed a Bosnian couple in a very gruesome way. I believe that the murder was committed with a knife. I ordered that they be brought in and that the case should be closed and that they should be prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was -- do you know if that was done, was a report written up? What further action was taken?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were taken into custody on the same evening and as I explained to you Zoran Mihajlovic, whom I had known for a long time and he was frequently close to me, I told him that he should follow that and that the criminal report should be sent promptly, that was within three days. So they were detained because we were allowed to detain someone for up to 12 hours, I believe. And I suggested to him to resolve this with the chief of the centre and Zoran came back and told me, well, Zoran actually just waved his hand and he said, you should try to see about this. And I told this to Zoran and Zoran wrote a decision, I believe I signed it, and after two days there was also a criminal report which had been drawn up and we handed everything over to the prosecutor's office. So these were a man and wife. They were the perpetrators. And also another man and wife had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Perpetrators were Serbs and the victims were non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were Bosniaks, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned that Zoran Mihajlovic had come back to you after trying to resolve it with his chief of centre. That chief of centre at the time would have been Zoran Cvijetic?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know why he wasn't able to get it resolved with his chief? Get it processed through his chief?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave a statement at the time, but I was a bit careless and I think this is noted in the comments, perhaps because these were Muslims and this is part of my explanation, but this was my conclusion which was unfounded. When you think about it now, they didn't have a single man in the administration. I think it was the beginning of May or the end of April I'm not sure, but immediately at the outset Zoran had come from the civilian sphere and he wouldn't have been able to draft that neither in terms of contents nor formally, and he couldn't have seen it done. That was probably the reason and that was why this Zoran Mihajlovic did everything that was necessary and these people were then brought in as appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. But that's not what you said in 2004; right? You offered an assumption in 2004?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please read it? Yes, yes, it says there I'm explaining now, I did it in an unfounded way and it was something that I assumed and to assume something and then charge somebody with it. If you read my statement you can say, well, I can conclude that that - I think that's how it's formulated - that this was the reason, but whether it was proper to draw such a conclusion well, and also considering, as I'm telling you now, that it was only in June and the question is whether they had a single man at the centre in June who was in charge of tasks of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I lost the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How long ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just this minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll just pause for awhile.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's back, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The assumption that you stated in 2004 was that you thought perhaps Mr. Cvijetic thought that Serbs should not be detained for killing Muslims, that's what you said then; right? And you made it clear that that was only an assumption?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends how one understands it. Another matter that is very important. In 2004 I was interviewed as a suspect, right, so all my focus was directed at trying not to incriminate myself. Thinking how I came into the position to be on such a list was something that I had to keep in mind. I wasn't really concentrated. When someone sends you messages you have to be cooperative or you may lose your job and to be so concentrated to be able at every moment, this is something that you have to take into account at all times. And also what I could observe in such conditions in war time, when there were hundreds of issues that I had to keep in mind pertaining to my family and everything else that was going on around, was I subjective in my observations? Of course I was. Could I always be objective when I judge something? People, you have to take this into even in most normal circumstances a man cannot -- two or three of us will interpret one thing differently, we'll all see it differently, this is why I say please do not take me to task for this. If I said I assumed then, please, don't use these assumptions because this is something very serious, and when I said that I did not take into account any one in my surroundings, I was just focusing on myself. So please try to understand me. Don't think that I'm trying to lie. As I was doing all of this you can see what I was doing, when it was difficult to do it, I stated everything now. Why do I think that it was exactly how it was done? I will tell you. And when I assume something, I won't go into any more assumptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, I will remind you to remember the interpretation, and you are speeding up again, so if you could pace yourself in terms of your answers. And Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: This is on at least three occasions in the course of today you have -- and the reason why I didn't intervene earlier is because I wasn't sure how to say it, I'm not sure how to say it now, but I'm not entirely satisfied that you have been proceeding correctly with what appears to you to be an inconsistency between the witness's testimony and his previous statement. So the -- I'm just bringing it to your attention. I'm not purporting to make any ruling now but just bring it to your attention. I'm not purporting to make any ruling now, I'm just bringing it to your attention to conform the manner in which you approach this to the rules of procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm listening, Your Honour, and I hear what you are saying. I really have one particular area in his prior statement from 2004 that I want to have an extended discussion with him about near the end, and I want to bring to your attention some jurisprudence from this Tribunal because I know with the witness ST-215, I had a discussion with your Judges about what use could be made of a prior inconsistent statement. I have some authority where I will try to persuade you that it's appropriate for me to -- if I ask him and he confirms having said something different previously than he says now, that I may be entitled to ask you to accept that prior statement not only for evidence of impeachment but also perhaps his substantive evidence depending on what showing I can make. But that's something I'm not at yet and I will get there, but I think that's the only other time I will ask a question about his prior transcript. And a specific reference therein.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember a man named Ivan Curak - I'm not sure I'm pronouncing that correctly - who was detained?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us who he was and when that happened?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was probably in May. It was one of the assistants of the interior minister, he was actually chief of one of the administrations and retired at the time when this happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where did this take place?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May, as I've told you. I think it was in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my question was where?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, where. In Vraca within the school complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what happened to him? What did you see happen?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was brought in to the ground floor with a rifle and a pistol. When he was searched the weapons were found. He was from Grbavica, he lived down there. So he was in the duty room, and when I came along I could see that the late Malovic had hit him and I reacted. I asked him what this was all about, and he said here he was found with weapons and he had a sniper sight on his gun because he was a hunter, but knowing the man, I knew that he was not a sniper. I'm not sure who was the duty officer, I said stop this, I told Malovic to leave the room, he grumbled a bit but he left. And this Curak was after that taken to Pale and after that he was exchanged. I'm not sure after how many days, so that was the gist of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you say the late Malovic, are you referring to Dusko Malovic?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who you knew to be the commander of the Special Police platoon from Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He appeared only then. They were a combat unit, some 20 to 30 men, and they were holding a line right behind the school, but they slept at the school. That is, their positions were right behind the school. I'm not sure how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Curak was a non-Serb?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. We talked about the thieving policemen that you referred to Mr. Kljajic. Who in 1992 in the RS MUP had the power or authority to remove a policeman for something like looting or thieving; do you know?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In practice it functioned the following way: The commander would say don't come in anymore because there weren't any rules and regulations to rely on or none that would be the foundation for launching disciplinary proceedings. And you didn't even have a stamp to put on a decision. So it was taken care of as we went along. You would have him return his equipment and weapons and tell him don't come in anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if the person to be removed or punished was an SJB chief, who in the RS MUP had the authority to punish or remove him?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's up to the minister or a person authorised by the minister. But at that time real removals, if you understand it in legal terms, there was no such thing because there weren't any underlying regulations or rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But as a practical matter, it could happen and did happen on occasion that SJB chiefs were removed or replaced; yes?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any such instance while I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. And I assume that your answer would be the same if the question were, who had the authority or power to remove a CSB head or an assistant minister? That would be the minister; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Just two or three miscellaneous questions before I get to the end. Did you ever see a group of Red Berets under the command of a man who was nicknamed Charlie?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Charlie and there were about three or four armed men always around him. He used to move about in a Pinzgauer vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where did you see Charlie and his men?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He used to come to Pale and he was billeted up there maybe at Kosuta or below Kosuta there are some apartments, I believe that he was billeted there. But they only stayed briefly. There was internal strife among them and it resulted in physical conflict. They shot at each other and after awhile they were no longer to be seen there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately when they were there in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must have been May. Whether they went into June, I'm not sure, so I suppose it was at the latter half of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you personally have any experience with anyone who you later learned was a member of what was known as the Yellow Wasp?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That has to do with my return from Belgrade. When I was crossing from Serbia to the RS at a place called Karakaj, the road didn't go through Zvornik but it went over Sapor and through Sekovici and on to Pale. There was a check-point at Karakaj where it later became clear, at least to me, the Yellow Wasps checked everything, or all traffic, all passengers, and we had to wait there. Combat vehicles would escort us there because there were frequent attacks. That's why the combat vehicles were there. There was a man with long hair. He said that he was a journalist and he interviewed people, and he saw me in a new car and said, well, thank God, here is a new car coming back from Belgrade, and I asked him what do you mean? He said, well all the new cars that go to Belgrade never come back, they stay there. So I was curious to know how he knew that and then he pulled out a notebook and started giving me the information of how many cars he had seen crossing the border without ever returning. I introduced myself to him as the assistant minister for crime prevention and detection, asked him whether he would give me that information, that notebook, and he agreed. Do you mean that incident, and I'm talking about with regarding the Yellow Wasps?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Do you remember hearing his name?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He introduced himself but I only remember him saying that he was a journalist. And he had long hair down to his shoulders and he wore boots. He was all dressed very smartly like an army officer. I sent one of my men down there, but on the following day there was my clash with the minister and I believe that inspector of mine never returned, either. He went on to Denmark or the Netherlands.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Two short questions before the break. What kind of car did you have?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Golf.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This would have been then on about the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. This is an appropriate point for the break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'd requested to address one procedural matter before the witness is brought in, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And also I think Your Honours have been alerted that there's a request for 20 minutes at the end the session concerning other procedural matters. I wanted to advise the court that I expect that on one area of questioning I have remaining with this witness cornering Dusko Malovic and the special unit that his answer will be substantially inconsistent with something he said in his statement in 2004, and I would propose because based on proofing and what's in the proofing note he agrees that he said what he said in 2004, but he says something different now, he recognizes it's different, and I want to put on the record what he said before by reading it out and then asking him if he can explain or what his explanation is for why what he is saying today is different. And then depending on what his answer is, asking him some questions about that explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Do I understand you when you adumbrated this earlier to say that there is jurisprudence which holds the Trial Chamber can accept the previous inconsistent statement instead of the live testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And may I bring that to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I would be very interested to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And let me do a little introduction. Oral evidence remains the primary and normal standard. And in accordance with the principle of orality that is expressed in Rule 89(F), prior statements of a witness should not be tendered into evidence where relevant portions thereof have been read out and entered on the record. So that's why I propose to enter it on the record. But your question is about whether that can substitute for viva voce testimony. It has been emphasised that a contention that viva voce testimony bars the admission of previous statements is incorrect as a matter of law. Citing a decision in the Seselj case, first of all a decision on the accused's submission 403 dated 4 November 2008 at paragraph 8, "Prior statements of a witness may be admitted into evidence when the party calling the witness intends to impeach their credibility, even where the witness also provided viva voce testimony." And the citation for that is "Seselj Decision on the Prosecution's Oral Motion Seeking the Admission into Evidence of Three Written Statements," it's dated 11 September 2008, at paragraph 9. "A Trial Chamber may exercise its discretion to admit a witness's previous inconsistent statement as hearsay evidence for the truth of its contents provided that it is relevant and sufficiently reliable to be accepted as probative." The citation for that is Popovic et al., "A Decision on Appeals Against Decision on Impeachment of a Party's Own Witness," 1 February 2008, at paragraph 31. "And ultimately the decision as to whether a particular piece of evidence will be admitted for the purpose of assessing a witness's credibility and/or for the substance therein must be left to the Trial Chamber's discretion," again citing that September 11, 2008 Seselj decision and the Popovic decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, obviously something to which careful consideration would have to be given, but do I understand you to be saying that as a part of where you are now headed with this witness is that you would be seeking to impeach him on a portion of his testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just what I anticipate his testimony is going to be about one particular topic concerning Dusko Malovic and his special unit providing security for the minister in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But aren't there certain conditions precedent to the calling party being able to do that, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I don't think the precedent here is so clear about whether in the past in the early days when I was here, I understood sometimes it was necessary for a party to show that the witness was hostile and ask leave of the Court to lead the witness and treat him as hostile. But -- and I don't have the authority on that in front of me, but it was my understanding and impression that that has been watered down some and that there is not an absolute bar against a calling party impeaching their own witness, particularly given the circumstances of these kind of cases where often times the witnesses we are calling are people who were members of the formations and either co-workers or subordinates or superiors of some of the people who are charged in the joint criminal enterprise. It's a factor we say that goes to weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Do we need to hear from Defence at this stage or should we wait to see what the application is and then hear what your response is? Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Whatever pleases the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Because it strikes me at this point your response may be premature in that we are in the realm of --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Anticipation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. So perhaps we could see where Mr. Hannis is and then we would hear from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, well, I was just -- whatever -- of course whatever pleases the Court. I just wanted to use the opportunity, maybe, because the witness is not here, and I think that might be more appropriate that we discuss this without the witness being present, but whatever is the Court's suggestion, I will gladly accept. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how near Mr. Hannis is to the -- to what he wishes to do, but even -- it still seems to me that he would have to lead the witness up to a certain point before he makes his application. The witness could always be excused while we pursue this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, and what I'm trying to do is lay a foundation for the argument I want to make when I make my anticipated application. And it's not something, as I see it, that you need to rule on today or next week or even, but I want to put in the record the necessary elements for me to be able to fashion my argument about why I think you should give more weight to a prior out-of-court statement than perhaps what he's going to say under oath today about a certain issue. But I'm not going to be able to make that argument if I can't ask him is that what you said before and why is what you are saying now different and what are the reasons for that difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just briefly, we do object that this be put on the record because so far the principles that were applied in this courtroom was that the witness statement was provided to the witness to refresh his memory and give a comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That is what I was alluding to. You would recall that when I mentioned to Mr. Hannis earlier, the way that he had put certain inconsistencies to the witness was not the way we had been doing it heretofore, and that is precisely the background on which I was relying, that the -- what we have said, as you have correctly articulated it, Mr. Zecevic, is that the witness has shown the statement and then asked for -- and then an appropriate question is phrased so what is -- and what doesn't end up being put into the record is the previous statement which may or may not be consistent and which may or may not -- there may or may not be an explanation for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This situation, I think is slightly different though. This is based on proofing and what's in the proofing note is that it is not going to refresh his memory because he is going to say, yes, I said that in 2004 but that's not correct, and it doesn't refresh my memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so could we have the witness return to the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- unless it wasn't clear, Mr. Zecevic, it seems to us that the first stage would be for counsel -- the calling counsel to refer to him in that manner, to confront the witness with the apparent contradiction, then we go on from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mr. Planojevic. Just a couple of remaining matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness Exhibit P732.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Coming up on your screen in a minute, Mr. Planojevic, is a document, I don't know you've seen before, but it's a decree on awarding of commendation and it lists a number of commendations for a number of members and units of the RS MUP. It's, I think, in 1993, and I want to ask you if you can comment on a particular item. If we go to page 13 of the English and it's page 9 of the B/C/S. And number 139 in this portion of the list, these are persons and units that are receiving a metal for the services to the nation and number 139 appears to be you, Dobrislav Planojevic, chief of SNB administration. Can you tell us about that, did you receive such an award or not?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was nominated for the award, but I wrote a letter expressing my unwillingness to receive it and I demanded to be taken off the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: To whom did you write and what was the nature of your unwillingness to receive that award?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the president decorates people by decree, I was nominated by my colleagues from the SNB. I thought that it wasn't the time for any commendations or awards and therefore I was unwilling to receive one. Actually, I may have written a sentence saying that one day I may give -- give an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And who was the president at the time that you wrote to?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Mr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you still have a copy of that letter or note that you wrote?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the last subject I wanted to cover with you is Dusko Malovic and his Special Police platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could show the witness Exhibit P984. This is at tab 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: This is a payroll slip for the special platoon from October 1992. You've already mentioned Dusko Malovic earlier in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in proofing we looked at some photos and you recognise some people that you knew as being members of his special unit. Looking at this list of names, do you recall any of these individuals as persons that you knew in 1992 as being a part of that Special Police platoon, besides Dusko Malovic?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I knew and I do know Boban Kezunovic, Nenad Stuparusic, Rajko Paunic, Danko Arbinja, Milenko Ecimovic, Zoran Jolovic, Predrag Bartula; he was a man who trained kickbox, though I never saw him in this unit. And that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think this is still marked as MFI and I would request that it be now non-MFI'd. I think any other objections to it go to weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't really see the nexus between this witness and the document, and I believe, if I correctly remember, the reason why it was MFI'd was precisely that it was shown again to the witness who didn't know anything about it except that can read the context and the names, knowing some of the individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, my argument is this document appears regular on its face and consistent with other payroll documents that we've seen, had authenticated and admitted into evidence. The connection that this witness give us is several of those individuals named on there were people he knew in 1992 as being members of the unit named therein, and therefore I think any other objection to it should only go to weight and not admissibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So Mr. Zecevic's recollection is incorrect in terms of the way that this document -- the reason why this document was only marked for identification previously?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Honestly, Your Honour, I can't speak to that. I don't recall who it was first showed to and where it got the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: My own recollection is that -- other payroll -- my own recollection accords with yours, Mr. Hannis, in terms of how other payroll lists have been dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I know many of those payroll documents were dealt with whom we had somebody who was on the list who said yes, that's me, and I was in that position in June 1992 and got paid, but we haven't brought anybody in from the special platoon but this is the next best thing I would argue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: By majority, Judge Harhoff dissenting, we agree to have the document admitted and marked. And I see Mr. Hannis shares my reluctance about how we non-MFI'd, I've never heard it expressed that way, or de-MFI a document, but whatever we do it is now entered as a regular exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Perhaps I should request that it be promoted to a full exhibit. I don't know. We'll find some term. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, were you aware of or do you know who by individual names or by title of units -- during 1992 who provided security, personal security for the Minister Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, we discussed this two or three times and you got angry because of my statement when you offered me to sign the document which I gave as a suspect. What's in that document is true. I claim that I saw these men in the presence of Mico Stanisic only on two occasions. Let me explain. If I remember properly, I think it was just then when we set off for that collegium meeting in Belgrade, we were travelling through Caparde, and there was an escort, vehicles that were escorted, he passed me by and the escort included 3 or 4 cars. I recognized some of the men, including Malovic, who were in full gear and they were the escort which was always provided on that section of the road. There were also combat vehicles to boot. And as for Mico Stanisic, I could conclude that that was him. And the other occasion was in 1994 at the collegium in Pale again as his escort. That was another occasion when Mr. Mico Stanisic was the minister, Malovic came to the collegium with him. And he was present, I think that his position then was a higher inspector because throughout the collegium meeting he was present. That is what I saw and what I said under the oath which I had already given. This is the only thing that I accept as true. I think I have told you enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that, but -- well, I have to discuss this with you now in court in front of the judges, so I understand clearly your position now is that at no time in 1992 other than this one occasion where you're saying some of the men of Malovic were providing an escort along that dangerous section of the road on one occasion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You recall that you were interviewed by representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor on June 8th and 9th, 2004, in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as you've reminded us, you were interviewed as a suspect at that time; right?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The OTP representatives were attorney Julian Nicholls, an investigator named Christophe Klebek, K-l-e-b-e-k, and a Nicolas Sebire, S-e-b-i-r-e. Do you remember that, it was three men?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as -- at the beginning of the interview, you remember they told you you were a suspect and they informed you of the rights you had?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: They told you that you were not a target of an investigation?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can I be a suspect if I'm not targeted. If I know anything about law, I find this to be illogical. There are many illogical things about this, Mr. Prosecutor. There are hidden messages which one does not see but which do reach you when you are a suspect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, LiveNote has been lost, they are trying to reconnect. It may take a minute we are told.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Perhaps while that's going on, I could have the usher hand the witness a copy of his interview from 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What page are we at, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the interview right now I'm just going to ask him a question on page number 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I have learned that even in the Tribunal a lawyer's minute has longer than 60 seconds, so although you've indicated that the OTP only requires 20 minutes at the end of the day's sitting to deal with whatever matters they wish to raise, I'm going to read that as half-hour and excuse this witness at 1.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think that's probably wise, Your Honour. I always tell my friends to take a lawyer's estimate of time and multiply it by two or three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We understand that the problem is not being corrected as quickly as we thought it would have been, but could we go on with the left-hand screen which is still working? Do counsel have a problem with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well honestly we do, but if there's no other way there's nothing we can do about it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The reason why I ask is because having regard to what Mr. Hannis has indicated what he is going to do, I was thinking that the inability of counsel to highlight and that sort of thing may have presented a problem, but if it isn't, we go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is precisely the problem that we have because we cannot highlight it in the LiveNote, but if it's not possible, I guess we need to go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I know if I were the one in the cross-examination seat at the time, I would want to wait until it's on, but if Mr. Zecevic is okay with me going on, I will. But I know that if our shoes were reversed, I would -- I really rely on it a lot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That's what I suspected and that's why I made the inquiry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I can be of assistance, Your Honours. Since it is obvious that my cross-examination will not start today obviously, then I will have enough time to -- when I receive the original transcript I can highlight it so then we can continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You are ahead of us, Mr. Zecevic. Yes, Mr. Hannis, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, you didn't have a lawyer at that interview, but you were aware that you had the right to have one and you said you were okay to proceed without one; correct?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did those three men treat you appropriately, respectfully, professionally?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, except for some questions which were leading and so on, so when you are giving an interview, you can read it in two different ways. So if they ask you isn't it so, it's normal that you will once say yes it is, or it's also normal that I would state my opinion, which does not have to be correct, my conclusion does not have to be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, do you agree that you said something different about Dusko Malovic and his men and their role as security escorts for Mr. Stanisic in 1992? What you said then is different than what you are saying now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, we understand that LiveNote is back.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I trust everybody it's back?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, if we could, I'd like you to go to page 92 in your transcript?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in English Your Honours, I'm going to start at page 88. I would indicate that the immediately preceding three or four pages in the interview are a question about the July 11th meeting and the witness is asked to identify each of those attendees who are listed, if he knew them and how he knew them, et cetera. And beginning at the bottom of 88, Mr. Sebire asked this question: "Were there any personal escorts from any of the attendants we have already mentioned, were there any driver's, secretaries?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Which line are you at?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at line 33 on page 88 in the English. And now I'm going on to page 89. Mr. Planojevic's answer was: "Mico was never walking without an escort and at least four guards, and when he was going through RS there were at least three --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is precisely my objection, Your Honours. That the witness has his copy and Mr. Hannis can ask him without citing the contents of his interview in the -- on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Zecevic, that Mr. Hannis was correct when he earlier said that this isn't like the refreshing memory situation, so to that extent, I was -- I was in error in agreeing with you on that point. But in as much as there is a contradiction that he is putting to the witness, then it doesn't matter and it may be of assistance to -- although the witness has the advantage of having it in front of him, it may be of assistance for Mr. Hannis to continue as he is doing now to read into the record the precise passage which he is, in his submission, is contradictory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, if I may just briefly address this. It is my understanding that the procedure we adopted in this court was that the counsel for who calls the witness can impeach the witness on the contents of its previous statement, but the impeachment goes to the credibility. It doesn't go to the context of his previous statement. Now, Your Honours, if the case is that not only it does refer to its credibility but also to the contents that my friend or the party calling the witness wants to rely first on the contents of the statement, plus to put the issue of credibility of the witness before you, Your Honours, then we have a problem because it is -- it is that party's witness, Your Honours. If this -- if this is true, the Prosecutor could have called this witness as 92 ter and give his contents of his statement, whatever it is, as a document. Now, they choose call him viva voce and in my understanding the only relevant, the only relevant testimony would be his viva voce testimony and not the other contents of his previous statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, it seems to me that there are a number of separate considerations which you are advancing contemporaneously and it seems to me that first thing -- that the problem, which is probably the wrong word, but the problem has to be dealt with sequentially, and the first step would be for the witness to be referred specifically to what appears to be a contradiction and see what his explanation is and, depending on his answer, then we go on from there. It may be that there is a perfectly logical, reasonable, and dare I say innocent explanation which the witness may have for what counsel perceives to be a contradiction but that has to be established, I would have thought, first of all, as to whether it is a contradiction. That having been done, then the next stage would be the challenge to the witness in terms of the correctness or otherwise of the testimony, the viva voce testimony as contrasted with the earlier statement, then comes the point where you seem to be. The arguments as to what the Chamber is to make of that at the end of the day. But I think that things have to be done in that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand and appreciate, Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, I trust I haven't confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I think -- I'm agreeing with you. I think precisely that's what needs to be done and what I'm trying to do. I would indicate just -- it's come to my attention that there was a sort of a related discussion about this topic on the 8th of October 2009 at page 1093 in connection with witness ST-181, where Judge Harhoff was talking about the situation and kind of the difference between a hostile witness which has certain connotations in common law verses perhaps calling them an adverse witness. But this is what I'm trying to do, I'm trying to lay the foundation. I need to put this in the record and, as you say, there may be an explanation that will clear it all up and explain why what's said today is really not different or if it is different, there's an understandable reason why it's different. But we can't do that until we see the difference between what's said today and what was said then, and so if I may, I'd like to read the rest of the answers on this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, in as much as we are up against the clock, should we -- aren't we in a position where we would be best advised to postpone this fascinating exercise until we resume next Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm sort of reluctant to give the witness five or six days to think about an explanation for why there's a difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I just assist. I'm here for the administrative matter, but it simply -- it will not take more than 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well, please proceed, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not sure where I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: "And when he was going through the RS there were -- there were at least three vehicles escorting him, so at least ten men. I assume that he also came there with that escort." Nicolas Sebire: "Do you know if his escort was formed comprised of police officers? Planojevic: "In the beginning, chief of his escort was a Abazovic, Goran, before the war he was in a special unit of BiH Ministry of the Interior; and his driver was Jasarevic, Zoran, all professional police officers. Question from Sebire: "Sorry, Jasarevic or Jasarovic? "Jasarevic," says the interpreter. Question: "Zoran?"

utterances.speaker: MR. PLANOJEVIC
utterances.text: "Da. So whenever he was going on some trip most often, I would see late Dusko Malovic. Nicolas Sebire: "He was a member of the escort?" Planojevic: "Yes, especially in those first two or three months of the war. Dusko Malovic, he had a group of something between 20 and 25 men, and they were all from Sokolac. And Zoran Cvijetic, as a head of the centre, brought those guys and Mico took them from Zoran." Nicolas Sebire: "And this group of 10 to 20 men -- sorry, 20 to 25 men, were they assigned to any special unit?" Planojevic: "In the beginning that was a like a combat unit that came with Zoran Cvijetic to Sarajevo. So for the first month they were protecting the line and they were participating in combat, combat activities. After that a certain number of men from that unit were taken by Mico, and I don't know the exact number but there were usually around 10 of them. When I was telling you that I visited minister in Kosuta, three or four of those guys were sitting in his cabinet wearing full gear, fully equipped. I didn't like it, I didn't like them being present during the meeting because I wanted to talk to him in private. But he said 'you speak freely because let them stay in.' Because I got an impression that he was also afraid of me so that he didn't want to let them go, which was really ridiculous to me." And I think that I'll stop there. Mr. Planojevic, you heard what you said in 2004 during that interview. Can you explain to the Judges why your answer today is different from what you said in 2004?

utterances.speaker: DOBRISLAV PLANOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, we are not talking only about today. When you offered me to sign the statement, I also said that it wasn't right. And now Your Honours, you try to decide whether what I say in my statement can be true. I said that in the first days that they were a combat unit, which is true. I believe that they lost their last man in late June in combat around Dobrinja, I believe his name was Glavonja because they went to the funeral because of the death of that man. So they were in combat almost until the end of June. And if you look at my statement that I only had three contacts with the minister and that I had never seen him anywhere, that this is contradictory to what is stated here. Could I have said then that these people, and I was focused on myself at the time, not minding much what I was saying about others, and I say with full responsibility that I saw these people only one time with Mico Stanisic. They were not really his security detail. They were his escort, making sure that he could pass. I spent time at Vraca and whenever I went to -- from Vraca I went either to Rogatica or to Belgrade. I never once did I see the then minister. So I cannot say that they were constantly with him, securing him. I can say that the people until the end of June were in combat around Grbavica and Vraca. I saw him on the 9th of July, probably, when they were his escort. I was in Belgrade for awhile and I said that I only once again saw Mico Stanisic in October, we went to his birth place and I went into combat. I didn't have an official position. Since that was the birth place of Mico Stanisic and we met, Abazovic and Jasarevic were with him then. That was in October. This is really the truth. If somebody were to analyse the whole statement and reads what it is stated here, it's all correct, but analyse the whole content, my movements, my contacts with the minister, even if it is true, I am in no position to assert that because I wasn't able to observe any of this. Mention is made of Kosuta. As far as I know they did go to Kosuta occasionally to rest, and I said that there were apartments there. And I cannot state with certainty that they were in the lobby because there is a front desk and possibly the people were there. I am not sure about that. Everything else is something I stand by even now. And this is really the whole truth. And imagine a position when you are faced with three people and they tell you that you are a suspect and as for the law, well, let me not go into that. So what I'm saying now I really stand by it. And if I -- if I can be proven wrong when saying that I was at a place or not, I will accept that. And I signed a statement but when we spoke at Nedzarici I didn't even see the statement. In May or June when we spoke, I arrived from Pale in the evening at 7.00 or 8.00, and I was told that I would get a digested version of my statement and that I should be prepared for an interview for the following morning. At 8.00 p.m. the interpreter, whose name I forget, brought me an envelope with 150 pages. To read that you'll need four or five hours, even without thinking about everything you said. I did skim through it and said that I had some minor objections and some minor remarks. And how did it all come about? Before I set up contact with the lawyers I pointed out the fact that this isn't true, I did so through the interpreter, didn't I, Prosecutor? But then I -- my feeling was that the Prosecutor didn't want to talk about that with me, and on the following day he said that I had been talked into that by my lawyers. It is my impression that the Prosecutor wanted me to come here to talk about that. Well, anyway, this is what I had to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, please forgive me for being perhaps a bit confused here, but since you are raising the issue of a contradiction, I would be grateful if you could clarify to me just where the contradiction is between the part that you read from his statement in June 2004 and what he has now explained, just to be sure that we are on the same line of understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I have fully understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand what he is saying now in 1992 the only time he saw Dusko Malovic and any of his men providing any kind of security or escort for the minister were when they were part of the group that was in the convoy traveling with the minister along a stretch of the road between Pale and Belgrade when the minister was going to the meeting on July 11th, 1992. And I think what he said in 2004 is quite different from that. Do I need to -- should I point out to you where I think it's different?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well, I'm trying to understand the importance of this contradiction because if it is only a question of the occasions in which the witness may have observed Mr. Malovic and the accused Mr. Stanisic together, then I wonder what the significance of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, it is and has been a contested issue in this case the exact function of Dusko Malovic and his unit and to whom they were subordinated, and we've heard some evidence about that from several witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In any event -- sorry -- in any event, Mr. Hannis, you've put the previous statement to the witness and he has given an explanation. Can you take this any farther? If at all there's anything left of this, mustn't this abide the end of the case in submissions and arguments?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think now that I have that in the record and we've heard his explanation, I have the arguments I want to make and can make about whether or how much weight you should give to this versus that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Oh, I thought that -- I misunderstood you, I thought that your next step would have been to invite us to substitute the -- but, thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I have one precise question in this regard for you. In the 2004 statement, you were giving an account of a very precise incident, if I may call it like that, in Kosuta. "Three or four of those guys," you said, "were sitting in his cabinet wearing full gear, fully equipped, I didn't like it, I didn't like them being present during the meeting because I wanted to talk to him in private. But he said you speak freely because let them stay, let them stay in because I got an impression that he was also afraid of me, that he didn't want to let them go away and it was really ridiculous to me." This is a very precise account with impressions and whatnot. And when I take what you said now about this, it is "mention is made of Kosuta. As far as I know, they did not go to Kosuta occasionally to rest. They did go to rest and I said that there were apartments there and I cannot state with certainty that they were in the lobby, because there is a front desk, et cetera." That first account of the incident of what happened in the cabinet of the minister and your impression you didn't like it, but you thought he was afraid of you, is that true or was that made up in 2004?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Abazovic was certainly sitting there in full gear. Abazovic, mind you, I don't think that he was ever a member of this unit and he was inside. I think Zoran also, and I don't know who was the third one, but that was what I didn't like. But by inertia I responded like that. Not knowing at the time and what did it mean to me then and what does it mean to me now, who was Mico's escort, whether it was one way or another I didn't believe this to be important, and I tried on three or four occasions to explain this to Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So this is true that there's no contradiction between what you said today and what you said there on that particular incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So, Mr. Hannis, are we at an end of this issue and we can excuse the witness until the court resumes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I think I would only have one other question and I can do that now or I can do that when he comes back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner had indicated 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So I think we better let her go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Planojevic, as would have been explained to you, your testimony is so expansive that it's going to occupy several court days, and again we've reached the point where we must take the adjournment for today to make the courtroom available for other work. Now, Monday, which would have been the ordinary day of resumption, is a holiday on the -- this Tribunal's schedule, observance of United Nations day. But for certain administrative reasons, this trial is unable to -- we are unable to resume on Tuesday or Wednesday, so when we rise in a quarter of an hour, we will not be resuming this trial until Thursday afternoon of next week and the -- although you are sworn as a witness and what I -- the cautions that I gave you yesterday still apply, I understand that arrangements have been made to permit you to travel back to your home and be returned in time for next Thursday, so we wish you a safe weekend and we will resume, as you would have heard Mr. Hannis say, he expects to wrap up his examination-in-chief shortly after you come back on Thursday afternoon. So the usher would now see you from the courtroom. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are just two matters. One requires us to go into private session very briefly. It's the shorter of the two.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If I can preface this by saying this is a very Friday afternoon application request. Your Honours will recall that Your Honours order that the Defence today provide us with the information relating to the three witnesses who were due to come next week and whether they now would stipulate to the adjudicated facts. One of them was witness ST-50 and the adjudicated fact to which he was to speak is fact 1326, where the last four lines were crossed out during the course of Your Honours consideration of that fact. And that's all that the witness was to speak to because the rest of the fact was left in. There was some confusion about whether or not it could be agreed by the Defence. However, it then was pointed out when we looked at the fact that those same four lines which were crossed out in fact 1326, appear uncrossed out in fact 1327. And we wouldn't have the temerity to suggest that the right hand didn't know what the left hand was doing when looking at those two facts, but the reality is, Your Honour, the -- we had decided -- we had actually noticed or the lawyer who was dealing with this particular set of facts had noticed that. We decided that, as we didn't really know what you intended, that we had better on the side of safety and line up the witness to deal with that particular fact. Or that part of the fact which you had crossed out even though it wasn't crossed out in the next fact. And can I say equally when we were writing out the adjudicated facts, the right hand didn't know what the left hand was doing either as it repeated the same part. So for safety's sake -- the Defence position on this is well we've got the fact anyhow, so you don't need us to agree it one way or another and you don't need the witness. Well, I think what we need to do is to be reassured that that's right. And for Your Honours to decide whether or not we have got the fact or we haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise, Ms. Korner. Page 84, line 25, did you say fact 1326 or 1236?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I hope I said 1326.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: There could be a rather simple solution to this. The question is, hearing what Ms. Korner said, does the Defence agrees that the Chamber takes judicial notice of this adjudicated fact, the one, the complete one?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, that's precisely the matter. You have ruled upon this and the contents of the fact are just in two facts instead of one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So therefore the four lines which Ms. Korner is talking about of the fact 1326 are already admitted by your decision as a part of the fact 1327.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And the Defence has --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, there's no -- those are exactly the same lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And the Defence has no problem with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we want to keep it as this so we can challenge it. We don't need to stipulate because it's already there and there's no need for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I fully understand the difference between -- that you are making now between agreed facts and adjudicated facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So if we don't have to go into the question for ourselves is there a contradiction between the two, and what did we mean to decide, and you agree with this being an adjudicated fact taken notice of by the Chamber, then problem solved. Then it is an adjudicated fact, not an agreed fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is an adjudicated fact. We confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I think what I heard Mr. Zecevic say, before we can go any further, is so we can challenge it. So if there is a challenge to this adjudicated fact, which hasn't emerged yet, but if there is a genuine challenge then we will still call the witness. And, therefore, we are in effect saying if the Defence don't agree this, then we will call the witness to deal simply with the part that was crossed out. He does not deal with the beginning of that fact 1326, but if there's a challenge to what's said on the 17th of August, a group of more than 80 Muslim men who were being detained in a school were transferred by police officers in camouflaged uniforms, then we will call the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I think this is a situation that is a situation for numerous adjudicated facts. The Defence doesn't -- I didn't hear the Defence say they are challenging it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that's -- I thought I heard Mr. Zecevic say then we can challenge it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, they can challenge it but that doesn't mean they do it. They can challenge all of the adjudicated facts but that doesn't mean that they are already doing it, and I take it that if the Defence doesn't say today we are challenging it, that is because they don't know yet whether they have reasons to challenge it or not. That goes for all adjudicated fact. So if it is an adjudicated fact, it's an adjudicated fact among what, a thousand other ones, and if it is challenged, we'll hear that it is challenged and we hear, we take it, and that's for reasons of fairness, that the Defence let us know about the challenge as soon as they know they will challenge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It seems that I have spoken a little bit on my own, Mr. Zecevic. So it is the Chamber's decision that the four lines are denied as adjudicated fact. It was an oversight. In one fact we didn't accept it and it was an oversight to accept it in the other one. So the decision is it is a denied adjudicated fact. And then the question stands, do you agree to stipulate on it or don't you, and if you don't, then Prosecutor has to call the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me try to understand now. So in fact, the fact 1327 that we have right now is not actually the adjudicated fact?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So the four lines of the fact 1327 now should be also deleted? Well, then you will have to give me a minute to discuss with my members of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's fine because Mr. Zecevic has to let us know about the other as well, so we'll just take it in the normal way. He doesn't have to tell us straightaway.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, thank you. That's -- that's -- I appreciate your help, Ms. Korner. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And that brings us to the end of the week's work and we trust that everyone has a safe weekend, and I remind you that we resume in the afternoon of the -- next Thursday in this courtroom.
